title: Redis: caching
seriesDescription: How to use Redis in system design interviews: the data model, durability limits, clustering, caching, distributed locks, leaderboards, rate limiting, geo search, streams and pub/sub, with the trade-offs interviewers probe.
description: Using Redis as a cache: key design, TTL versus eviction, memory limits, and the trade-offs around staleness.
source: Study notes: how to use Redis in system design interviews

questions.prompt: How do you cache a product in Redis?

options.text: Use a key like product:123 with a JSON blob or hash as the value.
options.why: Right: cache keys are Redis keys, cached values are Redis values.

options.text: Create a new table named product with a row per field.
options.why: Redis has no tables.

options.text: Store every product under the same key and filter on read.
options.why: That makes one huge hot key.

options.text: Use the product description text as the key.
options.why: Keys should be stable identifiers, not long content.

questions.explanation: Distribution across the cluster is trivial: more capacity means more nodes.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between TTL and an eviction policy?

options.text: TTL handles staleness per key; eviction frees memory when the instance is full.
options.why: Right: two different jobs.

options.text: They are two names for the same setting.
options.why: They solve different problems.

options.text: TTL frees memory under pressure; eviction expires keys on a timer.
options.why: That reverses them.

options.text: TTL applies only to lists; eviction applies only to strings.
options.why: Both are general mechanisms.

questions.explanation: Expiration guarantees you never read a key after its TTL; eviction decides what to throw away when memory runs out.

questions.prompt: Redis is out of memory and no eviction policy is configured. What happens by default?

options.text: Redis rejects writes once memory is full.
options.why: Right: it does not silently drop data.

options.text: Redis evicts the least recently used keys automatically.
options.why: That needs a policy such as allkeys-lru.

options.text: Redis doubles its memory using disk swap.
options.why: It does not grow on its own.

options.text: Redis deletes the oldest key regardless of settings.
options.why: Without a policy it refuses writes instead.

questions.explanation: For a cache, configure an eviction policy like allkeys-lru so old keys make room for new ones.

questions.prompt: True or false: Redis approximates LRU by sampling keys, which is good enough for a cache.

options.text: True
options.why: Correct: it samples rather than tracking exact order.

options.text: False
options.why: It does not track exact order.

questions.explanation: Tracking exact order is expensive. Sampling keeps the cost low and still evicts mostly cold keys.

questions.prompt: What is the cost of putting a small in-memory cache in each app server in front of Redis?

options.text: A second cache to keep coherent, so data may be stale up to its TTL.
options.why: Right: short TTLs on a small set of keys work best.

options.text: It removes the need for Redis from the design.
options.why: Redis still serves misses and shared data.

options.text: It makes every read slower because of extra hops without any extra configuration.
options.why: It removes hops for hits.

options.text: It guarantees strong consistency across app servers in the majority of deployments.
options.why: Separate caches drift.

questions.explanation: Client-side caching trades freshness for load reduction on hot keys.

questions.prompt: On a cache miss in the common pattern, what does the service do?

options.text: Reads from the database, then stores the result in Redis for next time.
options.why: Right: the usual read-through flow.

options.text: Returns an error because Redis has no data.
options.why: A miss is normal and falls back to the source.

options.text: Waits for Redis to fetch the data from the database itself in a typical production setup.
options.why: Redis does not know your database.

options.text: Deletes the database row to match the empty cache for most everyday workloads.
options.why: The database stays the source of truth.

questions.explanation: The database remains the source of truth. Redis is a fast layer in front of it.

questions.prompt: Which choice best describes where Redis fits for a read-heavy product page?

options.text: As a cache in front of the database, with TTLs to bound staleness.
options.why: Right: the most common deployment.

options.text: As the system of record, with the database removed under normal operating conditions.
options.why: Durability limits make that risky.

options.text: As a replacement for the CDN for static images as a general rule of thumb.
options.why: Different layer and different purpose.

options.text: As a message broker only, never for reads.
options.why: Caching is the most common use.

questions.explanation: The most common deployment of Redis is a cache.
